content: Scabies is a contagious skin infection caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei. The primary mode of transmission is direct skin-to-skin contact. Scabies can be classified into two main types based on the skin lesions observed: typical scabies infestation and crusted scabies (also known as Norwegian scabies). Crusted scabies is often associated with immunocompromised individuals. The hallmark symptom of scabies is intense itching, which worsens at night, accompanied by redness of the skin. Skin lesions of varying sizes are typically found in areas such as the webs of the fingers and toes, as well as the wrists. With appropriate antimicrobial therapy, the prognosis for scabies is excellent. Treatment should be extended to both the patient and close contacts, even if they are asymptomatic. Historically, the relationship between mite infestation and skin lesions was first described in 1687 by the Italian physician Giovanni Cosimo Bonomo. Cases of scabies have been documented in literature as early as 1853. In earlier times, sulfur-containing products, such as baths, vapors, or ointments, were considered the treatment of choice for scabies. The most common mode of scabies transmission is direct skin-to-skin contact. Other methods of transmission include sexual contact, particularly among men who have sex with men, and rarely through fomites or shared clothing. However, fomite transmission is more likely in cases of crusted scabies due to the higher mite burden. Cross-infectivity from other mammals, such as companion dogs, has also been reported but is rare. The life cycle of the mite involves survival off the host for 24–36 hours at 21°C. Female mites burrow into the epidermis at a rate of 0.5–5 mm per day, laying 2–4 eggs daily. Larvae hatch within 2–4 days and develop into adult mites within 10–14 days. The clinical manifestations of scabies, including intense itching, redness, and multiple skin lesions, are due to a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction by the host immune system. Histopathologically, scabies is characterized by mites surrounded by an inflammatory infiltrate of eosinophils, lymphocytes, and histiocytes. Crusted scabies is often associated with conditions such as Down syndrome, diabetes mellitus, HIV, HTLV-1, and leukemia, particularly in immunosuppressed individuals. The causative organism of scabies is Sarcoptes scabiei. Scabies must be differentiated from other dermatological conditions. The global prevalence of scabies varies widely, ranging from 200 to 71,400 cases per 100,000 individuals. It is estimated that there are 300 million cases of scabies worldwide. Scabies is more common in children and adolescents than in adults. The highest prevalence is observed in the Pacific and Latin America, while the lowest is in Europe and the Middle East. Risk factors for scabies include living in high-risk areas such as sub-Saharan Africa and indigenous communities in Australia and New Zealand, crowded living conditions, homelessness, poor hygiene, and immunocompromised states. Norwegian scabies, the severe form, is more likely to develop in immunocompromised individuals, such as the elderly, malnourished, and those with HIV or diabetes mellitus. If left untreated, scabies can lead to secondary bacterial infections of the skin and underlying soft tissue, which may result in severe complications such as sepsis, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, and rheumatic heart disease, particularly in immunocompromised hosts. Major complications include impetigo, skin abscesses, cellulitis, and necrotizing fasciitis. These secondary infections can progress to life-threatening conditions such as septicemia, renal failure, and rheumatic heart disease. The prognosis for scabies is generally excellent with prompt treatment. Antimicrobial therapy, such as topical permethrin or oral ivermectin, is effective in resolving the infection and associated itching within weeks. However, patients may experience worsening pruritus and erythema early during treatment as the body eliminates the parasite through natural shedding processes. Diagnosis of scabies involves a thorough history and physical examination. Key historical points include exposure to known cases of scabies, close contact with individuals with similar complaints (e.g., itching), daycare attendance in children, hospitalization history, and recent travel. The main symptoms include intense itching, worse at night, and red skin lesions, typically a few millimeters in size, found on the finger webs, wrists, elbows, axillae, buttocks, and groin. Physical examination may reveal burrows, papules, vesicles, bullae, and excoriations. Burrows are short, wavy lines created by female mites burrowing into the skin. Papules are small, erythematous lesions that may transform into vesicles or bullae over time. The characteristic distribution of scabies involves the web spaces of fingers and toes, wrists, and areolae in females and the penis in males. The back is usually spared, while facial and neck involvement is typically seen only in infants and children. Laboratory findings include serologic testing for Sarcoptes scabiei, which has high sensitivity and specificity. Elevated peripheral IgE levels are observed in patients with Norwegian scabies. The gold standard for diagnosis is the visualization of ova, feces, or mites under light microscopy. Skin biopsy can also confirm the diagnosis by identifying mites in the stratum corneum layer of the skin. Treatment of scabies involves antimicrobial therapy, primarily with topical permethrin or oral ivermectin. Permethrin 5% cream is applied to the entire body from the neck down and washed off after 8–14 hours. Oral ivermectin (200 µg/kg) is given in multiple doses and repeated after two weeks due to its limited ovicidal activity. Alternative treatments include lindane, though its use is limited due to toxicity concerns, including seizures and aplastic anemia. Lindane is contraindicated in pregnant and breastfeeding women, children under 10 years, and individuals with extensive dermatitis. For infants and young children, permethrin 5% cream is the preferred treatment, as lindane is not recommended for this age group. Crusted scabies requires a combination of topical scabicides (e.g., benzyl benzoate 25% or permethrin 5%) and oral ivermectin. Primary prevention of scabies involves promoting good hygiene and advocating for healthy living conditions, particularly in non-crowded environments. Secondary prevention includes initiating appropriate antimicrobial therapy promptly to eradicate the infection and prevent reinfection.
